title: First Aid Arrangements
summary: Prompt, properly given first aid can mean the difference between rapid or prolonged recovery, and even between life and death. Sites need trained first-aid providers, ready supplies, and a plan everyone knows.
talking_points: First aid is emergency care for an injury or sudden illness before emergency medical treatment is available.
OSHA requires trained first-aid providers at all workplaces if there is no infirmary, clinic, or hospital in near proximity that treats all injured employees.
Know who the trained first-aid providers are on your site and what to do if a coworker is hurt or ill.
First-aid supplies must be adequate, reflect the kinds of injuries that occur, and be stored where they are readily available in an emergency.
Sudden cardiac arrest can happen at work, for example from electrocution, low oxygen, or overexertion. Using an AED within 3-4 minutes can lead to a 60% survival rate.
Some OSHA standards require CPR training, including permit-required confined spaces and construction power transmission and distribution work.
If you are expected to give first aid as part of your job, the Bloodborne Pathogens standard applies to you and you need specific training.
First-aid plans should be written down and shared with all workers, including those who do not read or speak English.
site_hazards_to_check: First-aid kits missing, empty, or stocked with items that do not match site injuries
Kits stored where they are hard to reach in an emergency
No trained first-aid provider on the shift
No AED considered or available for sudden cardiac arrest
Unknown EMS response time to this location
Workers who do not know the first-aid procedure because of a language barrier
discussion_questions: Who are our trained first-aid providers today, and how do we reach them?
Where are the first-aid kit and AED, and what is in the kit?
How long would EMS take to reach us, and what do we do until they arrive?

flags: Verified against OSHA 3317: near-proximity rule, supplies 'readily available', AED 3-4 minutes / 60% survival, CPR-required standards list, BBP training, language-barrier note all present in source.

FIX: removed 29 CFR 1910.151 (general industry) because 1926.50 (construction medical services and first aid) is the construction equivalent and is already mapped. 1926.50 verified to exist and match (trained first-aid persons where no infirmary/clinic/hospital in near proximity; supplies). 1910.1030 kept: it is the bloodborne pathogens standard OSHA applies to construction (no 1926 BBP standard).

Non-blocking: source is a 2006 OSHA best-practices guide (advisory). Points 5, 6 are guide statements, not 1926 mandates; wording is not overstated. Talk states 1910.1030 reference only in citations; consider noting it applies to construction.
